claims.source: Compared to the control group, the amnesic group exhibited a loss of integration (increased average path length) in nodes of the MTL subsystem (Figure 7); namely, left and right parahippocampal cortex (MNI co-ordinates −28,–40,−12, β = −1.41, t = −3.51, p-FDR = 0.013 and MNI co-ordinates 28,–40,−12, β = −1.40, t = −3.53, p-FDR = 0.013, respectively), left retrosplenial cortex (MNI co-ordinates -14,-52,8, β = −0.75, t = −3.55, p-FDR = 0.013), left and right hippocampal formation (MNI co-ordinates −22,–20,−26, β = −0.93, t = −2.72, p-FDR = 0.033 and MNI co-ordinates 22,–20,26, β = −1.18, t = −2.99, p-FDR = 0.020, respectively), and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) (MNI co-ordinates 0, 26,–18, β = −1.52, t = −3.32, p-FDR = 0.020).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results and Figure 7 shows the affected nodes and their average path length differences.

claims.claim: The amnesic group exhibited increased average path length in the left temporal pole of the dmPFC subsystem.
claims.source: Increased average path length was also observed in the left temporal pole of the dmPFC subsystem (MNI co-ordinates −50,14,–40, β = −1.18, t = −3.34, p-FDR = 0.013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results and Figure 7 shows the affected node.

claims.claim: Local efficiency was significantly increased in three nodes: left posterior cingulate cortex, left parahippocampal cortex, and right retrosplenial cortex.
claims.source: Local efficiency was significantly increased in three nodes: left posterior cingulate cortex (left PCC) (MNI co-ordinates −8,–56,26, β = 0.35, t = 3.49, p-FDR = 0.020), left parahippocampal cortex (left PHC) (MNI −28,–40,−12, β = 0.45, t = 3.25, p-FDR = 0.037) and right retrosplenial cortex (right Rsp) (MNI 14,–52,8, β = 0.36, t = 3.45, p-FDR = 0.020).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results and Figure 8 shows the affected nodes and their local efficiency differences.

claims.claim: Differences in average path length from the control group mean in the left parahippocampal cortex, left and right hippocampal formation, left retrosplenial cortex, vmPFC, and left temporal pole significantly predicted the quantity of total internal (episodic) detail remembered by the amnesic group participants.
claims.source: Differences in average path length from the mean of the control group in the left PHC (β = 1.05, t = 4.69, p=0.018), left hippocampal formation and right hippocampal formation (β = 1.81, t = 7.87, p=0.004 and β = −1.55, t = −8.66, p=0.003, respectively), left retrosplenial cortex (β = 26.61, t = 12.55, p=0.001), vmPFC (β = −26.31, t = −11.55, p=0.001), and the left temporal pole (β = −1.70, t = −10.26, p=0.002) significantly predicted the quantity of total internal (episodic) detail remembered by the amnesic group participants on the AI.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports robust multiple regression analysis results linking network topology to behavioral performance.

claims.claim: CA3 volume and total internal detail were significantly correlated when collapsed across groups.
claims.source: CA3 volume and total internal detail were significantly correlated (Kendall's τ (30) = 0.283, p=0.028, two-tailed; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), such that lower CA3 volumes were associated with remembering less internal detail on the AI, when these variables were collapsed across group.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis results and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows the relationship between CA3 volume and internal detail.

claims.claim: The amnesic group exhibited no significant deficits on standardized neuropsychological tests outside of memory, with the exception of delayed verbal recall.
claims.source: Comprehensive assessment using standardized neuropsychological tests revealed that the scores for the amnesic group were comparable or significantly above normative data on composite measures of intelligence, attention, executive function, language, visuomotor skills, visuoconstruction skills, verbal memory, visual memory, and recognition memory (see 'Materials and methods' for individual subtest tests underlying the domain scores; Supplementary file 1a contains detailed results and N for each domain). Delayed verbal recall performance (which contributed to the verbal memory domain) was significantly different from normative data (N = 16, average z-score = −0.77, s.e.m. = 0.24, t(15) = –3.16, p=0.006), but above the threshold that typically indicates severe impairment (−1.67).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports neuropsychological assessment results and Figure 6 shows domain scores.

claims.claim: LGI1-antibody-complex LE typically presents with amnesia and seizures and leads to non-reversible chronic atrophy that is confined to the hippocampus.
claims.source: LGI1-antibody-complex LE typically presents with amnesia and seizures (Dalmau and Rosenfeld, 2014), and leads to non-reversible chronic atrophy that is confined to the hippocampus (Finke et al., 2017; Irani et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this characterization of LGI1-antibody-complex LE.

claims.claim: In model organisms, LGI1 is predominantly expressed in CA3 and DG subfields.
claims.source: In model organisms, LGI1 is predominantly expressed in CA3 and DG subfields (Herranz-Pérez et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study on LGI1 expression in model organisms.

claims.claim: Lesion and molecular imaging studies in rodents indicate that CA1 and CA3 enable the rapid storage and retrieval of recent (<1 month) contextual fear memories, whereas remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3.
claims.source: Lesion and molecular imaging studies in rodents indicate that CA1 and CA3 enable the rapid storage and retrieval of recent (<1 month) contextual fear memories, whereas remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3 (Denny et al., 2014; Guzman et al., 2016; Kesner and Rolls, 2015; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Lisman, 1999; Lux et al., 2016; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Rebola et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple rodent studies on the role of hippocampal subfields in memory.

claims.claim: In humans, damage to CA1, associated with transient global amnesia, impairs recent and remote autobiographical episodic retrieval.
claims.source: In humans, damage to CA1, associated with transient global amnesia (lasting, 8.3 ± 1.9 hr), impairs recent and remote autobiographical episodic retrieval (Bartsch et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the effects of CA1 damage in humans.

claims.claim: In a recent study of a single case involving focal damage to the human dentate gyrus and a portion of CA3, secondary to hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury, deficits were found in recent and remote memories.
claims.source: In a recent study of a single case involving focal damage to the human dentate gyrus and a portion of CA3, secondary to hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury, deficits were also found in recent and remote memories (Baker et al., 2016; Kwan et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites case studies on the effects of dentate gyrus and CA3 damage.

claims.claim: Standard systems consolidation and computational-based theories predict that new hippocampal-dependent episodic memories become reorganized into a distributed neocortical network, such that remote memories are no longer dependent on the hippocampus.
claims.source: In standard systems consolidation and computational-based theories of episodic memory, new hippocampal-dependent episodic memories become reorganized into a distributed neocortical network, such that remote memories are no longer dependent on the hippocampus (Bayley et al., 2005; Bontempi et al., 1999; Dudai and Morris, 2013; Kim and Fanselow, 1992; Kirwan et al., 2008; McClelland et al., 1995; Squire and Bayley, 2007; Takashima et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple theoretical and empirical studies supporting systems consolidation theory.

claims.claim: According to multiple trace theory, the transformation hypothesis, contextual binding theory, and scene construction theory, episodic memory is hypothesized to be continuously dependent on the hippocampus for as long as the memory retains spatial detail and context-specific episodic content.
claims.source: By contrast, according to multiple trace theory, the transformation hypothesis, contextual binding theory, and scene construction theory, episodic memory is hypothesized to be continuously dependent on the hippocampus for as long as the memory retains spatial detail and context-specific episodic content (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Maguire and Mullally, 2013; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Moscovitch et al., 2005; Winocur et al., 2010; Yonelinas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple theoretical studies proposing continuous hippocampal involvement in episodic memory.

claims.claim: The default network can be fractionated into a midline core, a MTL subsystem, and a dmPFC subsystem.
claims.source: Applications of graph theoretic analyses and clustering analysis techniques to rs-fMRI have revealed that the DN can be fractionated into a midline core (posterior cingulate cortex and anterior medial prefrontal cortex [amPFC]), a MTL subsystem (ventral medial prefrontal cortex, posterior inferior parietal lobule, retrosplenial cortex, parahippocampal cortex, and hippocampal formation), and a dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) subsystem (dmPFC, temporo-parietal junction, lateral temporal cortex, and temporal pole) (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study that parcellated the default network into subsystems.

claims.claim: The hippocampus acts as a major 'hub', linking different subnetworks that are involved in memory retrieval.
claims.source: CA3 damage was also hypothesized to affect the functional connectivity of regions that have been implicated in autobiographical episodic memory, because the hippocampus acts as a major 'hub', linking different subnetworks that are involved in memory retrieval.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states this as a rationale for examining functional connectivity, drawing on established knowledge about hippocampal function.

claims.claim: Lesions involving hubs such as the hippocampus or other regions within the medial temporal lobe lead to disruption in the functional connectivity of non-local brain regions.
claims.source: Lesions involving hubs such as the hippocampus or other regions within the medial temporal lobe (MTL) lead to disruption in the functional connectivity of non-local brain regions (Backus et al., 2016; Crossley et al., 2014; Mišić et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing that MTL lesions affect distant brain regions.

claims.claim: The default network is associated with episodic retrieval.
claims.source: Nodes and their pairwise ties or edges (the quantification of functional connectivity) were focused on the default network (DN) (Buckner et al., 2008; Buckner and DiNicola, 2019; Raichle et al., 2001), because the DN is associated with episodic retrieval (Raichle, 2015; Spreng and Grady, 2010).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies linking the default network to episodic retrieval.

claims.claim: The default network overlaps with a network of regions associated with autobiographical memory, including parietal regions, medial prefrontal cortex, MTL, and lateral temporal cortex.
claims.source: The DN also overlaps with a network of regions associated with autobiographical memory; namely, parietal regions such as posterior cingulate cortex/retrosplenial cortex, the medial prefrontal cortex, the MTL, and the lateral temporal cortex (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014; Buckner and Carroll, 2007; Cabeza and St Jacques, 2007; Greenberg et al., 2005b; Schacter et al., 2012; Spreng et al., 2009; Svoboda et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies linking the default network to autobiographical memory.

claims.claim: All data were collected at the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype with a median time of 4 years between symptom onset and study examination.
claims.source: All data were collected at the chronic phase of the LGI1-antibody-complex LE phenotype (time between symptoms onset and study examination: median = 4 years, range = 7), suggesting that the outcomes were unlikely to be mediated by short‐term compensatory processes.
claims.evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the timing of data collection relative to disease onset.

claims.claim: The inter-rater correlation coefficient for scoring the Autobiographical Interview was 0.97.
claims.source: The inter-rater correlation coefficient was calculated to be 0.97, across the internal and external detail scores, which is in line with the index study (Levine et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports the inter-rater reliability for the AI scoring.

claims.claim: The amnesic group participants were comparable to the control group participants in their susceptibility to tangents during narrative construction.
claims.source: Results from the analysis revealed that the amnesic group participants were comparable to the control group participants in their susceptibility to tangents during narrative construction (cumulative total tangents across five intervals: amnesic group = 0.20, control group = 0.63), which suggests that the deficits in the recollection of episodic detail were unlikely to reflect insufficiently supportive questioning during the adminstration of the AI.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of tangents during AI administration.

claims.claim: The amnesic group used a similar number of words to describe episodes as the control group.
claims.source: the use of a similar number of words to describe the episodes (amnesic group, total number of words = 106,047, mean number of words per interview = 6628, s.e.m. = 696; control group, total number of words = 97,654, mean number of words per interview = 6103, s.e.m = 500; t(15) = 0.59, p=0.56) suggests that the amnesic group autobiographical episodic memory deficit did not reflect a general impairment in verbal output (Barnett et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports word count analysis comparing the two groups.

claims.claim: The amnesic group exhibited intact verbal fluency on the Graded Naming Test.
claims.source: The absence of impairment in the retrieval of external (non-episodic, semantic) detail, intact verbal fluency on the Graded Naming Test (mean z-score = 0.75, s.e.m. = 0.28, t(15) = 2.71, p=0.016, two-tailed one-sample t-test)
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports performance on the Graded Naming Test.

claims.claim: The amnesic group exhibited preserved associative semantic memory on the Camel and Cactus Test.
claims.source: Evidence for a null group difference in external detail aligns with the more general preservation of associative semantic memory (Camel and Cactus Test) (mean z-score = 0.20, s.e.m. = 0.30, t(14) = 0.67, p=0.514, two-tailed one-sample t-test) (Bozeat et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports performance on the Camel and Cactus Test.

claims.claim: Delayed visual recall was intact in the amnesic group.
claims.source: By contrast, delayed visual recall (comprised of Rey Delayed Recall) was intact (average z = −0.08, s.e.m. = 0.20, t(15) = 0.41, p=0.685).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports performance on delayed visual recall tests.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in functional connectivity between the amnesic group and control group for seed regions in the visual network and somatomotor network with the rest of the brain at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
claims.source: The additional analyses were consistent with these results, because there were no significant differences in functional connectivity between the amnesic group and the control group for the seed regions in the visual network and somatomotor network with the rest of the brain, when assessed at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analysis results for control networks.

claims.claim: Functional connectivity of the left and right hippocampal seed regions with the rest of the brain were not significantly different between the amnesic group and control group at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
claims.source: Unlike the effects found with MTL and larger hippocampal lesions (Hayes et al., 2012; Henson et al., 2016; Rudebeck et al., 2013), two sample independent t-tests revealed that functional connectivity of the left and right hippocampal seed-regions with the rest of the brain were not significantly different between the amnesic group and control group, when assessed at a corrected p-FDR <0.05 threshold.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analysis results for hippocampal seeds.

claims.claim: A significant group difference in functional connectivity was found between the right hippocampus seed ROI and the left PCC, but this difference did not survive Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
claims.source: A significant group difference in functional connectivity was found between the right hippocampus seed ROI and the left PCC (t(27) = 1.75, p-FDR = 0.046). Hence, the only region that exhibited a between-group difference in functional connectivity with the hippocampus was the left PCC, but this difference did not survive Holm-Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports ROI-to-ROI functional connectivity analysis results.

claims.claim: None of the five control networks (somatomotor, visual, salience, ventral attention, and dorsal attention) exhibited altered topological properties in the amnesic group relative to the control group at p-FDR <0.05.
claims.source: In the amnesic group, none of these networks exhibited altered topological properties in any of the graph theoretic measures relative to the control group at p-FDR <0.05 (see Supplementary files 1c–1g for results at p-FDR <0.05 and p-uncorrected <0.05 analysis thresholds).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports graph theoretic analysis results for control networks.

claims.claim: Differences in local efficiency at the three affected nodes (left PHC, right retrosplenial cortex, and left PCC) did not significantly predict the quantity of internal (episodic) detail remembered by the amnesic group participants.
claims.source: Differences in local efficiency at each of these three nodes from the mean of the control group did not significantly predict the quantity of internal (episodic) detail that was remembered by the amnesic group participants (Supplementary file 1r).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports robust multiple regression analysis results for local efficiency.

claims.claim: Movement parameters were not significantly different between the amnesic and control groups.
claims.source: Movement parameters were compared between the amnesic and control groups using two-tailed t-tests and revealed no significant between-group differences in mean framewise displacement, with amnesic and control participants exhibiting means of 0.23 mm (s.e.m. = 0.07 mm) and 0.26 mm (s.e.m. = 0.07 mm), respectively (t(27) = 0.570, p=0.573).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports motion analysis results from fMRI data.

claims.claim: There were no significant correlations between altered topology and mean framewise displacement.
claims.source: There were also no significant correlations between altered topology and mean framewise displacement (p-values >0.4).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis between motion and network topology.

claims.claim: Dice similarities for hippocampal subfield segmentation were high, with a median of 0.79 for the amnesic group and 0.76 for the control group.
claims.source: Dice similarities (amnesic group median = 0.79, control group median = 0.76) and intra-class correlation-coefficient-based metrics (amnesic group median = 0.98, control group median = 0.97) across lateralized subfield volumes demonstrated a high degree of reliability in the output of two full repetitions of the segmentation protocol in the entire dataset.
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports reliability metrics for hippocampal subfield segmentation.

claims.claim: Inter-rater Dice Similarity Indices for hippocampal subfield segmentation were reliable, with median values of 0.75 for the amnesic group and 0.74 for the control group.
claims.source: Inter-rater Dice Similarity Indices (DSIs) of two independent raters for the amnesic group and control group were also reliable (median amnesic group and control group DSIs across all subfields: 0.75 and 0.74, respectively).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports inter-rater reliability for hippocampal subfield segmentation.

claims.claim: Left and right CA3 exhibited comparable volume loss of 29% in the amnesic group when contrasted against the control group.
claims.source: Notably, left (mean volume loss = -29%, SEM = 0.04) and right (mean volume loss = -29%, SEM = 0.03) CA3 exhibited comparable volume loss in the amnesic group (N = 15) when contrasted against the corresponding control mean CA3 volumes (N = 15).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports lateralized CA3 volume loss.

claims.claim: A relative reduction in CA3 volumes was observed in all amnesic group participants.
claims.source: A relative reduction in CA3 volumes to their matched control was observed in all amnesic group participants.
claims.evidence: The manuscript states that all amnesic participants showed CA3 volume reduction.

claims.claim: CA1 volume loss was not significant when the alpha criterion was corrected for multiple comparisons.
claims.source: Also in line with our prior study of 18 amnesic participants with LGI1-antibody-complex LE, CA1 volume loss was not significant when the alpha criterion was corrected for multiple comparisons (mean volume loss = -16%, F(1,28) = 5.25, p-uncorrected = 0.019, Cohen's d = 0.91).
claims.evidence: The manuscript reports CA1 volume analysis results.

claims.claim: The observed selectivity of CA3 volume loss is consistent with the anatomical localization of enrichment of LGI1 gene transcripts in CA3 of the adult human brain.
claims.source: The observed selectivity of CA3 volume loss is consistent with the anatomical localization of enrichment of LGI1 gene transcripts in CA3 of the adult human brain (Hawrylycz et al., 2012), the expression of LGI1 gene transcripts in mouse CA3 (Herranz-Pérez et al., 2010), and evidence of greater neuronal loss in CA3 compared to CA1 following seizures in homozygous LGI1 knockout mice (Chabrol et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on LGI1 expression and relates them to the observed CA3 volume loss.

claims.claim: CA3 exhibits particular vulnerability to excitotoxic lesions associated with seizures compared to CA1.
claims.source: When compared to CA1, CA3 exhibits particular vulnerability to excitotoxic lesions associated with seizures, given that IgG-containing LGI1 antibodies induce population epileptiform discharges either in CA3 pyramidal neurons in vitro (Lalic et al., 2011), or from complement-mediated fixation of bound antibodies (Bien et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the vulnerability of CA3 to seizure-related damage.

claims.claim: The chronic phase of LGI1-antibody-complex LE represents a compelling lesion model for studying the causal role of human CA3 in the hippocampal network.
claims.source: Evidence of selective anatomical damage associated with LGI1 pathogenesis suggests that the chronic phase of the disease represents a compelling lesion model for studying the causal role of human CA3 in the hippocampal network.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the utility of this patient population for studying CA3 function.

claims.claim: The duration of CA3 involvement in autobiographical episodic retrieval is at variance with evidence from model organisms that suggests remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3.
claims.source: The duration of CA3 involvement in autobiographical episodic retrieval is at variance with the evidence from model organisms that suggests that remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3 (Denny et al., 2014; Guzman et al., 2016; Kesner and Rolls, 2015; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Lisman, 1999; Lux et al., 2016; McNaughton and Morris, 1987; Rebola et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The manuscript compares the current findings to prior animal studies.

claims.claim: The loss of episodic detail for recent and remote memories is consistent with neurobiological accounts that predict damage to the human hippocampus affects retrieval for as long as the memory retains vivid, episodic detail.
claims.source: The loss of episodic detail for recent and remote memories (i.e., for all but the earliest remote memory) is consistent with neurobiological accounts that predict damage to the human hippocampus affects retrieval for as long as the memory retains vivid, episodic detail (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Nadel and Moscovitch, 1997; Winocur et al., 2007; Yonelinas et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The manuscript relates the findings to theoretical accounts of hippocampal function in memory.

claims.claim: The preservation of the earliest remote memories is consistent with the contention that these memories are remembered more frequently, re-encoded, and can be supported by neocortical representations.
claims.source: The preservation of the earliest remote memories is consistent with the contention that these memories are remembered more frequently, re-encoded, and can be supported by neocortical representations (Sekeres et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study and draws an inference about the nature of early remote memories.

claims.claim: Impaired recall of detailed episodic memories in the amnesic group could reflect a diminution in the ability to discriminate between individual mnemonic patterns and/or to track the precision of episodic retrieval for specific events with partial cueing.
claims.source: Impaired recall of detailed episodic memories in the amnesic group could thus, in part, reflect a diminution in the ability of these participants to discriminate between individual mnemonic patterns and/or to track the precision of episodic retrieval for specific events with partial cueing (Chadwick et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates about the computational mechanisms underlying the observed memory deficits.

claims.claim: The effects of the CA3 damage on default network topology may help to explain the gap between the small bilateral subfield damage and persistent episodic memory loss.
claims.source: The effects of the CA3 damage on DN topology may help to explain the notional gap between the small, by volume, bilateral subfield damage observed here and persistent episodic memory loss.
claims.evidence: The manuscript draws an inference about the relationship between anatomical damage and functional connectivity changes.

claims.claim: The reduction in functional integration in the amnesic group aligns with the impact of damage to hub regions having a disproportionate effect on global efficiency.
claims.source: The reduction in functional integration — that is, the capacity to transmit information with less attenuation — in the amnesic group aligns with the impact of damage to hub regions, such as the hippocampus, having a disproportionate effect on global efficiency (Hwang et al., 2013 Albert et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the effects of hub damage and relates them to the observed findings.

claims.claim: The loss of integration in parahippocampal cortices is likely to have interfered with the operations necessary for remembering episodic detail.
claims.source: Parahippocampal cortices support context reinstatement (Diana et al., 2013) and remote memory (Lux et al., 2016), thus the loss of integration in parahippocampal cortices is likely to have interfered with the operations necessary for remembering episodic detail.
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on parahippocampal function and draws an inference about the impact of altered connectivity.

claims.claim: Integration between the affected regions and other parts of the core autobiographical network is particularly important for successful episodic retrieval.
claims.source: Integration between the affected regions and other parts of the core autobiographical network is particularly important for successful episodic retrieval (Westphal et al., 2017), and is likely to impact on the capacity of hippocampal-neocortical ensembles to support the reconstruction and elaboration that underscores autobiographical episodic retrieval (Barry and Maguire, 2019; Greenberg et al., 2005a; Piolino et al., 2009; St-Laurent et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on network integration and episodic retrieval.

claims.claim: Functional coupling between the hippocampus and retrosplenial cortex has been implicated in the initial reconstruction of the episodic context and detail as a memory is selected and accessed.
claims.source: For example, functional coupling between the hippocampus and retrosplenial cortex has been implicated in the initial reconstruction of the episodic context and detail as a memory is selected and accessed (Inman et al., 2018), and supports the consolidation of events (Bird et al., 2015; Staresina et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on hippocampal-retrosplenial interactions in memory.

claims.claim: Increases in local efficiency may alter connectivity with immediately surrounding regions that support the regulation of learning, consolidation, and retrieval, and could reflect adaptive functional reorganization.
claims.source: Increases in local efficiency may alter connectivity with immediately surrounding regions that support the regulation of learning, consolidation, and retrieval, and could reflect adaptive functional reorganization, possibly involving the reassignment of nodal roles.
claims.evidence: The manuscript speculates about the functional significance of increased local efficiency.

claims.claim: In model organisms, the inhibition of rodent CA1 can lead to selective compensatory changes in anterior cingulate cortex activity, which are associated with remote contextual memory.
claims.source: In model organisms, the inhibition of rodent CA1 can lead to selective compensatory changes in anterior cingulate cortex activity, which are associated with remote contextual memory (Goshen et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study on compensatory changes following CA1 inhibition in rodents.

claims.claim: Increases in local efficiency of between 85% and 270% have been observed in structural connectivity studies of left temporal lobe epilepsy, attributed to a compensatory mechanism that maintains connectivity despite the loss of connections in hub regions.
claims.source: Increases in local efficiency of between 85% and 270% have been observed in structural connectivity studies of left temporal lobe epilepsy, and attributed to a compensatory (perhaps maladaptive) mechanism that maintains connectivity despite the loss of connections in hub regions (DeSalvo et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study on local efficiency changes in epilepsy.

claims.claim: The effects of hippocampal and MTL damage on resting-state networks have variable scalar extents across mixed aetiologies.
claims.source: The effects of hippocampal and MTL damage, which are observed across mixed aetiologies, on RSNs have variable scalar extents (Hayes et al., 2012; Heine et al., 2018; Henson et al., 2016; Rudebeck et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing variability in the effects of MTL damage on brain networks.

claims.claim: The observed scalar extent of altered network topology aligns with evidence that simulated lesions involving hub regions can lead to non-extensive effects on topological organization.
claims.source: Also in line with the observed scalar extent of altered network topology is evidence that simulated lesions involving hub regions can lead to non-extensive effects on topological organization, whereas damage to regions that connect different network modules (connectors) can result in widespread effects that affect whole-brain network organization (Gratton et al., 2012; He et al., 2009; Honey and Sporns, 2008).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on the effects of hub versus connector lesions and relates them to the current findings.

claims.claim: Larger-scale effects on graph theoretic measures of functional connectivity have been reported following more extensive damage.
claims.source: Larger-scale effects on graph theoretic measures of functional connectivity have, however, been reported following more extensive damage (Henson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing more widespread effects with extensive damage.

claims.claim: Alterations in connectivity between the hippocampus and the posterior cingulate cortex are likely to disrupt autobiographical memory.
claims.source: Alterations in connectivity between the hippocampus and the posterior cingulate cortex are likely to disrupt autobiographical memory, because functional connectivity between the hippocampus and the posterior cingulate cortex has been implicated in episodic autobiographical remembering (Sheldon et al., 2016; Sheldon and Levine, 2013).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites studies on hippocampal-PCC connectivity and draws an inference about the impact of altered connectivity.

claims.claim: More extensive damage to the hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and temporal pole can lead to significant differences in functional connectivity that are limited to the default network.
claims.source: More extensive damage to the hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and temporal pole can lead to significant differences in functional connectivity that are limited to the DN (Hayes et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study on the effects of more extensive MTL damage.

claims.claim: Other studies have observed dysfunction in multiple large-scale brain networks following hippocampal damage.
claims.source: Other studies, however, have observed dysfunction in multiple large-scale brain networks following hippocampal damage, such that functional connectivity was decreased in the salience network and increased in the dorsal and ventral DN, sensorimotor network, and higher visual networks relative to that in control participants (Heine et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing widespread network effects following hippocampal damage.

claims.claim: White matter connectivity appears to be unaffected by LGI1-antibody-complex LE.
claims.source: It is important to note, however, that white matter connectivity appears to be unaffected by LGI1-antibody-complex LE (Finke et al., 2017).

results.result: The study recruited 16 participants with chronic amnesia due to LGI1-antibody-complex LE (mean age 64.2±4.81 years, 3 females) and 16 age- and education-matched healthy controls (mean age 62.3±3.23 years). All amnesic participants were seizure-free, clinically stable, and tested at the chronic phase (median 4 years post-onset).
results.evaluation: There is a critical discrepancy in C3 where the abstract states 6 females in the control group but the methods state 2 females, undermining the reliability of demographic reporting. This inconsistency raises concerns about data accuracy and quality control in the manuscript.

results.result: High-resolution 7.0-Tesla MRI with manual hippocampal subfield segmentation revealed bilateral CA3 volume loss of 29% in the amnesic group compared to controls (F(1,28)=14.52, p=0.001, Cohen's d=1.39), with all amnesic participants showing CA3 reduction. CA1 volume loss (-16%) was not significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Segmentation reliability was high (Dice similarities: 0.79 amnesic, 0.76 control).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C40-C44 provide converging evidence from volumetric analysis with appropriate statistical testing, correction for multiple comparisons, and reliability metrics. The selective CA3 damage is well-documented with high inter-rater and intra-rater reliability, supporting the anatomical specificity of the lesion model.

results.result: Whole-brain voxel-based morphometry at 7.0-Tesla revealed no significant gray matter volume loss outside the hippocampus in the amnesic group, with no other lesions detected. This finding replicates prior studies from the authors' laboratory and other groups studying LGI1-antibody-complex LE.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C92, C109-C110 consistently demonstrate focal hippocampal damage using appropriate whole-brain analysis methods (VBM with FWE correction p<0.05). The convergence with multiple prior studies strengthens confidence in the anatomical specificity of the lesion.

results.result: The amnesic group exhibited temporally ungraded retrograde amnesia for internal (episodic) detail spanning up to ~50 years prior to CA3 damage, with the exception of the earliest remote memory (0-11 years) which was intact. Post-hoc analyses revealed intact earliest remote memory (F(1,30)=0.250, p=0.621) but loss of internal detail across remaining intervals (group: F(1,30)=23.25, p<0.0001, η²p=0.437).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C100-C101 are supported by appropriate statistical analyses with clear main effects and interactions. The pattern of preserved earliest remote memory but impaired other remote and recent memories is well-documented with adequate sample size (N=16/group) and proper correction for multiple comparisons.

results.result: The memory deficit was specific to episodic (internal) detail, with preserved semantic (external) detail across time intervals (F(1,30)=1.24, p=0.275), comparable word production, intact verbal fluency (Graded Naming Test z=0.75, p=0.016), preserved associative semantic memory (Camel and Cactus Test z=0.20, p=0.514), and similar susceptibility to tangents during narrative construction.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C28-C31 provide converging evidence for the specificity of the episodic memory deficit through multiple complementary measures. The preservation of semantic memory, verbal output, and narrative structure supports that the deficit is not due to general cognitive or language impairment.

results.result: Comprehensive neuropsychological assessment revealed no significant deficits outside of memory, with the exception of delayed verbal recall (z=-0.77, p=0.006, but above severe impairment threshold). Delayed visual recall was intact (z=-0.08, p=0.685), and recognition memory was preserved, indicating the deficit was specific to episodic retrieval rather than general memory or cognitive impairment.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C32, C102-C105 demonstrate appropriate neuropsychological characterization with standardized tests and normative comparisons. The pattern of selective episodic memory impairment with preserved recognition and other cognitive domains is well-documented and consistent with focal hippocampal damage.

results.result: Graph theoretic analysis of resting-state fMRI revealed increased average path length (reduced functional integration) in MTL subsystem nodes including bilateral parahippocampal cortex, bilateral hippocampal formation, left retrosplenial cortex, vmPFC, and left temporal pole. Differences in average path length in these nodes significantly predicted total internal detail remembered (robust multiple regression: left PHC β=1.05, p=0.018; left HF β=1.81, p=0.004; right HF β=-1.55, p=0.003; left Rsp β=26.61, p=0.001; vmPFC β=-26.31, p=0.001; left TempP β=-1.70, p=0.002).
results.evaluation: While C8-C9 report significant group differences in network topology with appropriate FDR correction, C11's regression results are concerning. The extremely large beta coefficients (e.g., β=26.61 for retrosplenial cortex) and the mix of positive and negative associations are difficult to interpret mechanistically. The claim that increased path length in left PHC and left HF predicts better memory (positive β) contradicts the theoretical framework that reduced integration impairs memory. Additional validation and clearer interpretation are needed.

results.result: Local efficiency was significantly increased in three nodes: left posterior cingulate cortex (β=0.35, p-FDR=0.020), left parahippocampal cortex (β=0.45, p-FDR=0.037), and right retrosplenial cortex (β=0.36, p-FDR=0.020). However, differences in local efficiency at these nodes did not significantly predict internal detail remembered.
results.evaluation: Claims C10 and C37 are internally consistent, showing altered local efficiency that does not predict behavior. The finding is appropriately corrected for multiple comparisons and the null behavioral relationship is clearly stated, though the functional significance of increased local efficiency remains speculative.

results.result: Seed-to-voxel and ROI-to-ROI functional connectivity analyses revealed no significant differences between groups for hippocampal seeds or control network seeds (visual, somatomotor) at p-FDR<0.05. Only the right hippocampus-left PCC connection showed a difference (p-FDR=0.046) that did not survive Holm-Bonferroni correction. Five control networks (somatomotor, visual, salience, ventral attention, dorsal attention) showed no altered topological properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 appropriately report null findings with proper statistical thresholds and correction for multiple comparisons. The specificity of effects to the default network MTL subsystem is supported by the absence of changes in control networks and seed-based analyses.

results.result: CA3 volume and total internal detail were significantly correlated when collapsed across groups (Kendall's τ(30)=0.283, p=0.028), with lower CA3 volumes associated with less internal detail remembered.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 reports a significant correlation when collapsing across groups, but this approach is problematic. The correlation may be driven primarily by group differences rather than a true continuous relationship. The manuscript notes non-significant correlations within each group separately, suggesting the collapsed analysis may be misleading. A more appropriate analysis would examine whether CA3 volume predicts memory performance within the amnesic group specifically.

results.result: Motion parameters during fMRI acquisition were not significantly different between groups (amnesic: 0.23±0.07mm, control: 0.26±0.07mm, t(27)=0.570, p=0.573), and there were no significant correlations between altered topology and mean framewise displacement (p>0.4).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 appropriately address a critical confound in resting-state fMRI analysis. The comparable motion between groups and lack of correlation between motion and network measures support that the observed functional connectivity differences are not artifacts of head movement.

results.result: LGI1-antibody-complex LE typically presents with amnesia and seizures, leading to non-reversible hippocampal atrophy. LGI1 is predominantly expressed in CA3 and DG in model organisms and humans, with CA3 showing particular vulnerability to excitotoxic lesions from LGI1 antibodies. The observed selectivity of CA3 volume loss is consistent with LGI1 expression patterns and evidence from knockout mice, making this a compelling lesion model for studying human CA3 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C15, C45-C47, C87-C91 provide appropriate background and mechanistic context from prior literature. The convergence of evidence from human gene expression, animal models, and in vitro studies supports the biological plausibility of selective CA3 damage in this patient population.

results.result: The duration of CA3 involvement in autobiographical episodic retrieval (up to ~50 years) is at variance with evidence from model organisms suggesting remote memories depend on CA1 but not CA3. In rodents, CA1 and CA3 enable recent (<1 month) memory retrieval, but remote memories depend on CA1 not CA3. In humans, CA1 damage from transient global amnesia impairs both recent and remote memories.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18, C48 appropriately contextualize the current findings within prior literature, accurately representing the discrepancy between rodent and human studies. The comparison highlights the novelty of the current findings while acknowledging limitations in cross-species translation.

results.result: The pattern of memory loss is inconsistent with standard systems consolidation theory (which predicts remote memory independence from hippocampus) but consistent with theories proposing continuous hippocampal dependence for episodic detail (multiple trace theory, transformation hypothesis, contextual binding theory, scene construction theory). The preservation of earliest remote memories is consistent with these memories being more frequently rehearsed and supported by neocortical representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20, C49-C50 appropriately interpret the findings within competing theoretical frameworks, accurately representing both systems consolidation and continuous dependence theories. The interpretation is supported by the data pattern showing temporally ungraded amnesia except for the earliest memories.

results.result: The impaired recall of detailed episodic memories could reflect diminished pattern separation/completion computations supported by CA3. The deficit was specific to episodic detail with preserved semantic detail, consistent with hippocampal damage effects. The impact on remote versus recent memories may differ because remote memories undergo more extensive reconsolidation and reconstruction.
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C93-C95 provide reasonable mechanistic speculation about CA3 computational functions, but remain largely speculative. While the cited literature supports CA3's role in pattern separation/completion, the manuscript does not directly test these computational processes. The specificity of the deficit (C94) is well-supported, but the mechanistic interpretation requires additional empirical validation.

results.result: The effects of CA3 damage on default network topology may explain the gap between small anatomical damage and persistent memory loss. Reduced functional integration in MTL subsystem nodes (parahippocampal cortex, retrosplenial cortex, vmPFC) likely interfered with operations necessary for episodic retrieval, as these regions support context reinstatement, memory consolidation, and reconstruction of episodic detail.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 provide a coherent interpretation linking anatomical damage to functional network disruption and behavioral deficits. The interpretation is supported by appropriate citations and aligns with the empirical findings, though the causal chain remains inferential.

results.result: Increases in local efficiency may reflect adaptive functional reorganization, possibly involving reassignment of nodal roles. In model organisms, CA1 inhibition leads to compensatory changes in anterior cingulate cortex. Increases in local efficiency of 85-270% have been observed in temporal lobe epilepsy, attributed to compensatory mechanisms maintaining connectivity despite hub damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are largely speculative about the functional significance of increased local efficiency. While the cited literature (C58-C59) supports the possibility of compensatory reorganization, the manuscript provides no direct evidence that the observed changes are adaptive versus maladaptive, and C37 shows these changes do not predict memory performance.

results.result: The scalar extent of altered network topology (limited to MTL subsystem) aligns with evidence that hub lesions can have non-extensive effects, while connector lesions cause widespread disruption. More extensive MTL damage can affect multiple networks or be limited to the default network, with variable outcomes across studies depending on lesion extent and etiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 appropriately contextualize the current findings within the broader literature on network effects of brain lesions. The interpretation that focal CA3 damage produces limited network disruption is consistent with the empirical findings and theoretical models of hub versus connector damage.

results.result: White matter connectivity appears unaffected by LGI1-antibody-complex LE. Functional connectivity can reflect signaling within the underlying structural network, suggesting future studies should examine anatomical pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C66 and C114 appropriately note the limitation that structural connectivity was not examined in the current study, while citing evidence that white matter is preserved in this patient population. The suggestion for future work is reasonable given the relationship between structural and functional connectivity.

results.result: CA3 (along with CA2 and DG) are input structures associated with encoding, while CA1 is an output structure for retrieval. In healthy adults, CA3 volume correlates with memory differentiation efficacy, while CA1 volume does not correlate with episodic retrieval. fMRI studies suggest time and space context are represented across multiple hippocampal subfields. Volumetric studies show MTL volumes correlate with remote and recent autobiographical memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C71 provide appropriate background from prior literature on hippocampal subfield functions and structure-function relationships. The citations accurately represent the state of knowledge, though the manuscript notes challenges in interpreting single subfield volume-behavior relationships.

results.result: Human CA3 may be a default activator of remote episodic memories participating in their maintenance throughout recall. CA3 damage likely impairs engagement with neocortical memory traces because CA3 enables association of signals from different brain regions. The results highlight the important role of MTL subsystem integration in episodic memory. Different multiscale brain circuits are recruited during recent and remote memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 mix speculation (C72), reasonable inference (C73), and appropriate interpretation (C74-C75). While C73-C75 are supported by the data and literature, C72's claim about CA3 as a "default activator" is highly speculative and based on a single rodent study (Goshen et al., 2011) that examined CA1, not CA3.

results.result: The known timing, discrete onset, and monophasic nature of autoimmune encephalitis suggest hippocampal function was intact during encoding of pre-morbid memories. Therefore, impaired retrograde memory likely reflects disruption of CA3-mediated retrieval mechanisms rather than encoding/consolidation difficulties.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 provide a reasonable inference about the nature of the memory deficit based on disease characteristics. The logic is sound: if hippocampal function was intact when memories were formed, then the deficit must reflect retrieval impairment. This strengthens the interpretation of the findings.

results.result: All autobiographical memories were verified against collaterals with no evidence of confabulation found. Inter-rater reliability for Autobiographical Interview scoring was high (ICC=0.97), consistent with the original validation study.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C27 demonstrate appropriate quality control measures for the behavioral assessment. The verification against collaterals and high inter-rater reliability support the validity and reliability of the autobiographical memory data.

results.result: Hippocampal and CA3/DG activity measured by fMRI has been associated with remote autobiographical memory retrieval across wide time intervals (mean range -2.5 days to -32.3 years). Early memories are described as gist-like, qualitatively different from other remote memories, and can be supported by extra-hippocampal regions. The earliest intact remote memory may not be CA3-dependent, though it was not detectably schematized based on external/internal detail ratios.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 appropriately contextualize the finding of preserved earliest remote memory within the literature on memory transformation over time. The analysis of external/internal detail ratios (C99) provides empirical support that these memories were not qualitatively different, though the interpretation remains somewhat uncertain.

results.result: The specificity of impairment accompanying CA3 damage is consistent with the hypothesis that hub region damage generates specific cognitive deficits, while connector region damage causes broader deficits. Focal CA1 damage from transient global amnesia was associated with memory deficits but intact naming, conceptual knowledge, and attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C108 appropriately interpret the pattern of selective memory impairment within network neuroscience frameworks. The comparison to CA1 damage effects provides useful context, though C107 is somewhat speculative about connector regions.

results.result: CA3 is not a main output structure but has outputs via the fimbria that can bypass CA1, suggesting CA3 damage likely involves changes in functional connectivity of non-local brain regions. Evidence from rodent CA1 inhibition indicates selective compensatory changes can occur in anterior cingulate cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 provide appropriate anatomical and functional context for why CA3 damage would affect distributed brain networks. The inference about non-local effects is supported by the anatomical connectivity and the empirical findings of altered default network topology.

results.result: fMRI and neuropsychological studies indicate autobiographical and laboratory-encoded memories are dissociable. The behavioral results are compatible with the hypothesis that autobiographical event retrieval is qualitatively different from other episodic retrieval under some conditions. However, remember-know responses and personally familiar stimuli can activate autobiographical recall regions, and retrieval orientation can modulate the distributed network supporting autobiographical retrieval.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C118 appropriately acknowledge the complexity of relating laboratory-based memory tasks to autobiographical memory. The discussion recognizes both the potential dissociation and the overlap between different forms of episodic memory, providing a balanced interpretation.

results.result: All data were collected at the chronic phase of LGI1-antibody-complex LE with a median of 4 years between symptom onset and study examination, suggesting outcomes were unlikely to be mediated by short-term compensatory processes.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is well-supported and important for interpretation. The chronic phase testing (median 4 years post-onset) strengthens the conclusion that the observed deficits and network changes represent stable, long-term consequences of CA3 damage rather than acute or transient effects.
